cards.title: The Security Mental Model
cards.teaser: Security is not about eliminating risk — it is about making deliberate trade-offs between what you protect, from whom, and at what cost. Getting the mental model right before writing a line of defensive code is the most important thing a developer can do.

runs.text: Most developers encounter security as a checklist: use HTTPS, hash passwords, sanitize inputs. These are correct tactics, but they are not a mental model. A tactic applied without a model fails the moment an attacker finds the gap between your checklist items.
The foundational mental model has three parts:

items.text: Identify your assets: user data, financial records, session tokens, source code, infrastructure credentials. Not all assets are equal. A social media app's highest-value asset may be its user graph; a fintech app's highest-value asset is its transaction ledger.

Different attackers have different capabilities, motivations, and patience. A script kiddie running automated scanners is not the same threat as a nation-state APT group with months to invest. Your defenses must be calibrated to your actual threat landscape.

Security has real costs: development time, user friction, operational complexity. A bank is right to require MFA for every transaction; a recipe site is not. Perfect security that is unusable is not secure — users route around friction, creating worse vulnerabilities.

runs.text: The 2019 Capital One breach illustrates all three. The asset was 100 million customer records in S3. The threat actor was a former cloud provider employee with specialized knowledge of misconfigured WAF rules. The cost of defense — restricting EC2 metadata service access — was near zero. The failure was not technical sophistication; it was a gap in the threat model.

Adam Shostack's Threat Modeling (2014) formalizes this as the STRIDE model. But before any framework, the three questions above are the ones that force you to think like a defender rather than a builder.
Security is about three questions: what are you protecting, who is trying to take or break it, and how much effort is it worth spending to stop them? Every security decision flows from those answers.

cards.title: Same-Origin Policy
cards.teaser: The Same-Origin Policy is the browser's foundational isolation rule — it prevents a page at one origin from reading data from another origin. Without it, every malicious site you visit could silently read your email, your bank balance, and your session tokens.

runs.text: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) was introduced with Netscape Navigator 2.0 in 1995 as a direct response to the emerging threat of cross-site data theft. It is, arguably, the most important security boundary the browser enforces.
An origin is defined by three components — all three must match for two URLs to share an origin:

items.text: are different origins. A page served over HTTP cannot read from its own HTTPS counterpart.
are different origins, even though they share a parent domain.

runs.text: SOP restricts what a script running in one origin can do with responses from another origin. Specifically, it blocks read access to response bodies from cross-origin requests — but it does
not
block requests from being sent. This is the source of CSRF vulnerabilities: a malicious page can trigger a state-changing request to your bank, even though it cannot read the response.

SOP has deliberate exceptions: images, stylesheets, and scripts from other origins can be loaded (which is how CDNs work). These exceptions are why Subresource Integrity (SRI) exists — to verify the content of cross-origin resources you embed.

Michal Zalewski's The Tangled Web (2011) documents the SOP's many inconsistencies and browser-specific deviations in exhaustive detail. The rule is conceptually simple; the implementation is a patchwork of historical decisions and browser quirks.
Two URLs share an origin only if their scheme, host, and port all match. The browser uses this rule to prevent pages from reading each other's data — if origins mismatch, no peeking at the response.

cards.title: Origin vs Site
cards.teaser: Origin and site are not the same thing — and confusing them breaks your security model. An origin is scheme + host + port (strict). A site is scheme + eTLD+1 (looser). Cookies use site boundaries; SOP uses origin boundaries.

runs.text: The distinction between origin and site trips up even experienced developers, yet it is load-bearing for understanding cookies, CORS, and modern isolation features like COEP and COOP.

items.text: are different origins — same-origin policy treats them as strangers.
= scheme + eTLD+1. Where eTLD (effective Top-Level Domain) accounts for entries in the Public Suffix List.
is on the Public Suffix List.

runs.text: Why does this matter in practice? Cookies are scoped to a site by default (the
Domain
attribute uses site-level matching). This means a cookie set by
app.example.com
is sent by the browser to
api.example.com

— they are same-site, even though they are cross-origin. This is how many session-sharing architectures work, and how many CSRF attacks succeed: the browser sends the cookie cross-site because the attacker is targeting a same-site endpoint from a different origin.
The
SameSite
cookie attribute (introduced in 2016) was built precisely to tighten the gap:
SameSite=Strict
prevents cookies from being sent on any cross-site request;
SameSite=Lax
allows top-level navigation GETs. Chrome defaults to Lax since 2020.

An origin is the exact scheme + host + port triple. A site is the scheme + registered domain (eTLD+1), which groups subdomains together. Cookies use site-level matching; the Same-Origin Policy uses origin-level matching — and the gap between them is where many attacks live.

cards.title: Threat Actor Taxonomy
cards.teaser: Not every attacker is trying to exfiltrate your entire database. Calibrating your defenses to the right threat actor — script kiddie, opportunistic, targeted, insider, nation-state — is the difference between rational security investment and paranoid over-engineering.

runs.text: Security defenses are not one-size-fits-all. The cost-effective response to an opportunistic attacker is very different from the response to a nation-state adversary. The five-tier taxonomy:

items.text: — runs publicly available exploit toolkits against mass targets. Low skill, opportunistic, motivated by notoriety. Defence: patch known CVEs promptly, maintain basic input validation. If your unpatched Drupal site gets hit by Drupalgeddon2, a script kiddie did it.

— automated scanning and credential stuffing at scale. Financially motivated. Moves on quickly if defenses resist. Defence: rate limiting, MFA, breach-credential detection. The 2021 Twitch leak enabled waves of opportunistic gaming account takeovers.

— specifically choosing your organization as a target. Has time and resources to probe for bespoke vulnerabilities. Defence: threat modeling against your specific asset profile, red teaming, anomaly detection.

— a current or former employee, contractor, or vendor with legitimate access. Can be malicious or accidental. Defence: least privilege, audit logging, separation of duties, offboarding procedures. The 2019 Capital One breach was an insider-adjacent threat: a former cloud provider employee exploited privileged access.

— state-sponsored advanced persistent threat groups (APT28, Lazarus Group, Cozy Bear). Virtually unlimited resources, months of patience, zero-day budget. Defence: assume compromise; focus on detection and containment rather than prevention.

runs.text: The critical question is: which tier is in your realistic threat landscape? A startup's recipe app faces script kiddies and opportunistic attackers. A healthcare company faces all five. A government contractor faces nation-states by definition.

Capability vs motivation: nation-state actors have the highest capability but may not be motivated to attack you. Insider threats have lower technical capability but extraordinary access. Map both axes when building your threat model.

Threat actors range from automated script kiddies to nation-states with zero-day budgets. Most organizations face script kiddies and opportunistic attackers every day, and targeted attackers occasionally. Designing defenses for the wrong tier wastes money or leaves real gaps.

cards.title: The CIA Triad
cards.teaser: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three properties every security control is ultimately protecting. Every attack violates at least one. Getting clear on which property is at risk in a given scenario is the first step toward a proportionate response.

runs.text: The CIA triad is not jargon — it is a classification system that forces precision. When the Equifax breach exposed 147 million Social Security numbers in 2017, the primary violation was
confidentiality
. When attackers tampered with SolarWinds build artifacts in 2020, the violation was
integrity
. When the 2016 Dyn DDoS attack took down Twitter, Spotify, and Reddit for hours, the violation was
availability

items.text: — information is accessible only to those authorized to see it. Threats: data exfiltration, eavesdropping, credential theft, excessive logging. Controls: encryption at rest and in transit, access control, data minimization.

— data and systems are modified only by authorized parties through authorized processes. Threats: SQL injection, supply chain tampering, CSRF, log manipulation. Controls: input validation, signing (code, data, commits), audit logs with write-once storage.
— systems are accessible to authorized users when needed. Threats: DDoS, ransomware, resource exhaustion, cascading failures. Controls: rate limiting, CDNs, redundancy, incident response plans.

runs.text: The triad is also a source of tension. Full end-to-end encryption maximizes confidentiality but can impair availability (you cannot scan encrypted traffic for malware). Audit logs maximize integrity evidence but create confidentiality risk if logs contain PII. Recognizing these tensions is part of the security trade-off work.
Some frameworks extend CIA to CIAA (adding Authenticity) or CIAAAN (adding Non-repudiation). For web applications, the three-property model is sufficient for most analysis.

CIA: Confidentiality means only authorized eyes see the data; Integrity means only authorized changes are made; Availability means the system is reachable when needed. Every attack violates at least one — naming which one focuses your defense.

cards.title: Defense in Depth
cards.teaser: Defense in depth means layering security controls so that no single failure is catastrophic. If the firewall is breached, the application still validates input. If the app is compromised, the database still enforces row-level security. Every layer buys time and limits blast radius.

runs.text: The term originates from military strategy — force attackers to penetrate multiple lines of defense rather than a single fortified perimeter. In software security, the same principle applies: assume every individual control will eventually fail, and design so that failure is not fatal.
A classic web application defense-in-depth stack:

items.text: — firewall, WAF, DDoS mitigation. Blocks known malicious IPs and traffic patterns.
— input validation, output encoding, parameterized queries, authentication, authorization.
— encryption at rest, column-level encryption for PII, row-level security in the database, minimal permissions for the app's DB user.
— hardened OS images, no root processes, secrets in a vault (not environment variables), network segmentation.
— logging, anomaly detection, alerting. Assumes breach has occurred; focuses on minimizing time-to-detection.

runs.text: The Equifax breach (2017) failed defense in depth dramatically. The initial vector was an unpatched Apache Struts CVE (network/application layer failure). But the attacker then moved laterally for 76 days undetected because internal network segmentation was absent and monitoring was insufficient — layers 4 and 5 were effectively missing. 147 million records were exfiltrated.

Defense in depth is not the same as defense in redundancy. Adding three firewalls is not defense in depth — it is one control duplicated. Defense in depth requires diverse controls at different abstraction levels.

Defense in depth means assuming any single security control will eventually be bypassed, so you stack independent controls at different layers. Breaching one layer shouldn't give the attacker everything — they still have to break through the next.

cards.title: Principle of Least Privilege
cards.teaser: Give every user, process, and service the minimum access it needs to do its job — and nothing more. Least privilege contains the blast radius of any compromise: a breached process with narrow permissions can steal less than one with broad permissions.

runs.text: The principle of least privilege (PoLP) was articulated by Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder in their 1975 paper "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems." Fifty years later, most production systems still violate it routinely.
Common least-privilege violations in web applications:

items.text: Database user with full admin rights

— the application only needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on specific tables. Instead the DB user is a superuser. When the app is compromised, the attacker can drop tables, read system catalogs, and write files.
— a Lambda function needs to read one S3 bucket. Instead it has full S3 access plus EC2 describe permissions. The Capital One breach was partly enabled by an overprivileged EC2 role.
— API keys created for a long-departed contractor remain active. Opportunistic attackers find them in old config files committed to Git.
Admin UI accessible to all authenticated users
— a user-facing role can reach admin endpoints because no authorization check distinguishes user from admin. This is a horizontal privilege escalation waiting to happen.

runs.text: The discipline: when granting access, start from zero and add only what is explicitly required. Audit and rotate credentials on a schedule. Use time-bounded tokens where possible. Apply PoLP to humans, services, and infrastructure components equally.

Least privilege and zero trust are closely related. Zero trust extends least privilege to network access: no implicit trust based on network position, every request must be authenticated and authorized regardless of source.
Least privilege: every user and process gets exactly the access they need, and nothing extra. When something gets compromised, narrow permissions mean the attacker has less to work with.

cards.title: Attack Surface
cards.teaser: Your attack surface is everything an attacker can interact with — every endpoint, input field, API, dependency, and admin interface. You cannot defend what you haven't mapped; you cannot shrink what you haven't measured.

runs.text: The attack surface concept was introduced by Michael Howard at Microsoft in 2003 as part of the trustworthy computing initiative. It is deceptively simple: the attack surface is the set of all points where an unauthorized user can enter data, extract data, or trigger behavior.
Attack surface components in a typical web application:

items.text: — open ports, protocols, firewall rules, exposed management interfaces (Redis without auth, Elasticsearch on a public IP).
— HTTP endpoints, REST/GraphQL APIs, WebSocket connections, form inputs, file upload handlers, URL parameters, HTTP headers the app reads.

— every npm/pip/Maven package you import. A vulnerable dependency is part of your attack surface even though you didn't write it. Log4Shell (2021) was a dependency surface attack: a logging library used by hundreds of thousands of Java applications contained a critical RCE.
— phishing targets, social engineering vectors, employees with admin access.
— data stored in S3 buckets, databases, logs, backups. Misconfigured S3 bucket ACLs exposed thousands of companies' data in 2017-2019.

runs.text: Shrinking the attack surface is one of the highest-return security activities. Disable unused endpoints. Delete dead code paths. Remove unused dependencies. Restrict which services are internet-facing. Every feature removed from the surface is a feature that cannot be exploited.

OWASP's Attack Surface Analysis Cheat Sheet provides a structured process for inventorying and prioritizing surface components. Map your surface before you start hardening — you will find things that should not exist.

The attack surface is every entry point an attacker could use: endpoints, inputs, dependencies, admin panels, open ports. Map it, then shrink it — every piece you remove is a piece that can't be exploited.

cards.title: The Security Trade-Off Triangle
cards.teaser: Security, usability, and cost form a triangle where optimizing for any two comes at the expense of the third. The best security decisions are explicit trade-offs — not accidental ones made under time pressure.

runs.text: The security trade-off triangle is sometimes called the "CIA-Cost" model or the security-usability-cost trilemma. The insight is uncomfortable but necessary: maximizing security costs more and frustrates users; minimizing cost introduces risk; maximizing usability usually means reducing friction, which means fewer security checks.

items.text: High security + high usability = high cost.
Hardware security keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) are extremely strong and user-friendly — but require purchasing and distributing hardware, building enrollment flows, and maintaining recovery processes.
High security + low cost = low usability.
Forcing a 32-character random password with rotation every 30 days and no password manager support is "secure" on paper, but users write passwords on sticky notes — net security is worse.
High usability + low cost = low security.
No MFA, simple passwords, long session lifetimes. Easy to build and easy to use — and a credential-stuffing nightmare.

runs.text: The practical implication: every security control must be evaluated not just on whether it improves security, but on whether it degrades usability enough to cause user behavior that defeats the control. Bruce Schneier has described this as "security theater" when controls impose real friction with minimal real protection (e.g., removing shoes at airports).

Rational security investment starts by placing your application on the triangle explicitly: what is the asset value, who is the target user, and what is the acceptable friction level? Then choose controls that fit the triangle, rather than adding every available control and hoping usability survives.
Security, usability, and cost form a triangle: you can only fully optimize two. The right response is to make the trade-off deliberately and explicitly, not to pretend you can have all three at once.

cards.title: Trust Boundaries
cards.teaser: A trust boundary is any point where data crosses from a higher-trust context to a lower-trust one — or vice versa. Every trust boundary is a potential attack vector. If you don't know where your trust boundaries are, you cannot validate inputs correctly.

runs.text: The concept of trust boundaries is central to Adam Shostack's threat modeling methodology. A trust boundary is a line in a data flow diagram where two components with different trust levels exchange data. Whenever data crosses a trust boundary, it must be validated, sanitized, or authorized.
Common trust boundaries in web applications:

items.text: — the most fundamental boundary. All data from the browser is untrusted: URL parameters, POST bodies, cookies, HTTP headers. Validate everything. Assume the user is an attacker.
— SQL queries constructed with user input cross a trust boundary. Parameterized queries enforce this boundary correctly. String concatenation does not.
— microservices calling each other. "Internal" does not mean trusted. An attacker who compromises Service A can impersonate it to Service B unless mutual authentication (mTLS) is enforced.
— responses from external APIs are untrusted. An API you call could be compromised (supply chain), or you could be MITM'd without certificate pinning.
— user-controlled data used in file paths must be sanitized (path traversal). User-controlled data used in shell commands must be escaped or avoided entirely (command injection).

runs.text: Every SQL injection, XSS, and command injection attack is fundamentally a trust boundary violation: untrusted data was used in a privileged context without proper sanitization. Map your trust boundaries before you map your threats.

A trust boundary is where data moves between components with different trust levels — browser to server, server to database, service to service. At every boundary, the receiving side must validate what it receives rather than assuming the sender was honest.

cards.title: Authentication vs Authorization
cards.teaser: Authentication (AuthN) answers "who are you?" Authorization (AuthZ) answers "what are you allowed to do?" Confusing these two produces some of the most dangerous bugs in production — IDOR vulnerabilities, privilege escalation, and mass account takeovers.

runs.text: Authentication and authorization are distinct concerns that must be implemented separately and checked independently.

items.text: — verifies identity. "Is this request from who it claims to be from?" Mechanisms: passwords + MFA, OAuth 2.0 / OIDC tokens, SAML assertions, API keys, mTLS certificates. A passed authentication check means: "I have verified the caller's identity."

— verifies permission. "Is the verified identity allowed to perform this action on this resource?" Mechanisms: RBAC (role-based access control), ABAC (attribute-based), ACLs, policy engines (OPA, Cedar). A passed authorization check means: "The verified identity is permitted to do this thing."

runs.text: The canonical AuthZ failure is an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). A user is authenticated (identity verified), requests
GET /api/orders/12345

, and the server returns the order — but never checks whether order 12345 belongs to that user. Authentication passed; authorization was never performed. OWASP lists Broken Access Control as the #1 web application security risk as of 2021.
Common patterns:

items.text: — a normal user accesses admin-only functionality. AuthN correct, AuthZ missing.
— a user accesses another user's data by guessing resource IDs. AuthN correct, AuthZ incomplete.
— attacker removes signature, sets alg:none, server accepts. AuthN bypassed entirely.

runs.text: Authentication and authorization must be checked on every request, not just at login. A valid session token proves identity; it does not grant permission to every resource.

Authentication asks "who are you?" and verifies identity. Authorization asks "are you allowed to do this?" and checks permission. Being logged in (AuthN) doesn't automatically mean you can access every resource — that's what AuthZ checks, and forgetting it causes most access control bugs.

cards.title: The Security Mindset
cards.teaser: The security mindset is adversarial thinking — actively looking for what could go wrong rather than assuming everything works as designed. It is a skill that must be deliberately practiced, and it is the single biggest difference between a developer who writes secure code and one who does not.

runs.text: Bruce Schneier wrote in 2008: "Security requires a different way of thinking about the world. It requires thinking like an attacker — creatively, maliciously, and in ways that the designer never intended." This is the security mindset in one sentence.

Builders think about the happy path: "how will a legitimate user use this feature?" Attackers think about every other path: "what happens if I send negative quantities? What if I replay this request? What if I modify this JWT? What if I enumerate sequential IDs?"
Concrete adversarial thinking questions for any feature:

items.text: Identifying who is motivated to attack a feature focuses your threat model.
What does this assume that an attacker could violate?
Every implicit assumption in code is a potential vulnerability. "This endpoint assumes the userId in the JWT matches the userId in the URL" — does it verify that assumption?
SQL metacharacters, path traversal sequences, very long strings, binary data, Unicode edge cases, negative numbers, null bytes.
Error messages that include stack traces or SQL query fragments give attackers a detailed map of your internals. Failure paths are part of the attack surface.
Can this be abused at scale?
Rate-limiting gaps, missing idempotency, no CAPTCHA on high-cost operations — individually minor, devastating at automated scale.

runs.text: The security mindset is not paranoia — it is structured skepticism applied to your own work. The goal is not to assume everything is compromised; it is to identify which assumptions are the most dangerous to hold.

The security mindset means deliberately asking "how could this be abused?" for every feature you build. Builders think about the happy path; attackers think about every other path. The skill is training yourself to think both ways at once.

cards.title: Compliance vs Security
cards.teaser: Passing a compliance audit and being secure are not the same thing. Compliance is a point-in-time checkbox exercise; security is a continuous practice. The Equifax breach happened while Equifax was PCI DSS compliant. Compliance is the floor, not the ceiling.

runs.text: Compliance frameworks — PCI DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FedRAMP — represent codified minimum standards for protecting specific types of data in regulated industries. They exist because, without mandatory floors, too many organizations do nothing.
But compliance has structural limitations that make it insufficient as a security strategy:

items.text: A SOC 2 report covers a specific period and set of controls. The attacker does not wait for the next audit window.
"We have a WAF" satisfies a control. A misconfigured WAF that passes known payloads satisfies the same control. Compliance checks presence; security checks effectiveness.
PCI DSS 3.2 did not address container security. HIPAA does not address machine learning model privacy risks. Frameworks update slowly; attackers do not.
A PCI scope reduction means moving card data to a tokenization provider — which is smart — but it does not make the rest of the application secure. It makes it out of scope.

runs.text: Equifax (2017) was certified PCI DSS compliant at the time of the breach. The compliance requirement for TLS/SSL was satisfied. The Apache Struts patch was within the defined patching window — barely. Compliance passed; 147 million records were stolen.

The correct relationship with compliance: meet it because it is required, then go further because compliance alone is insufficient. Use compliance audits as forcing functions for documentation and process — but use threat modeling, red teaming, and continuous monitoring as your actual security posture.
"We're compliant" is a legal statement. "We're secure" is an engineering claim that requires ongoing evidence. Never confuse the two in a post-mortem.

Compliance is a set of minimum rules that must be met — security is the practice of actually protecting your systems. Equifax was compliant and still lost 147 million records. Compliance is the floor you must reach; security is what you build above it.
